comparison: Perfect agreement on NMF clustering validation (C52-C60). Both evaluations support the consistency between NMF and original classification methods. OpenEval notes a potential Ki67 contradiction with C45, while peer reviewers accept the methodology without raising this concern.

Perfect agreement on nomogram development (C79-C80). Both evaluations support the prognostic modeling approach. OpenEval provides more detailed assessment of AUC values and their clinical interpretation, while peer reviewers implicitly accept the methodology as 'solid and validated.'

Perfect agreement on LEP biological mechanisms (C86-C92). Both evaluations support the mechanistic interpretation based on cited literature. OpenEval explicitly notes the correlative rather than causal nature of the evidence, while peer reviewers accept the biological plausibility without raising concerns.

Perfect agreement on PTTG1 biological mechanisms (C93-C100). Both evaluations support the mechanistic context from prior literature. OpenEval notes the lack of mechanistic validation in RPLS specifically, while peer reviewers accept the explanations without questioning this limitation.

Strong agreement on LEP/PTTG1 biomarker identification (C61-C63, C71-C72, C7, C103). Both support the machine learning approach and biomarker utility. OpenEval raises concerns about potential overfitting given extremely high AUC values, while peer reviewers describe the classification as 'valuable and simplified' without expressing this concern.

Strong agreement on DEG analysis and pathway dysregulation (C33-C39, plus C4, C25, C31-C32 in peer review). Both evaluations support the bioinformatic analyses. Peer reviewers emphasize 'solid and validated methodology' and 'substantial sample size,' while OpenEval focuses on internal consistency of the data.

Strong agreement on biomarker-based clinical features (C64-C70, plus C8-C11 in peer review). Both support the clinical associations. OpenEval notes marginal significance for surgery times and tumor size reversal requiring investigation, while peer reviewers accept the prognostic findings without raising these specific concerns.

Strong agreement on two-subgroup characterization (C40-C48, plus C5-C6, C27, C49-C51 in peer review). Both evaluations support the pathway-based classification and clinical differences. OpenEval provides detailed assessment of statistical analyses, while peer reviewers emphasize the metabolic vs. cell cycle signatures and clinical significance.

Agreement on DEG analysis between subgroups (C49-C51). OpenEval evaluates this separately as validation of G1/G2 classification, while peer reviewers group it with the broader subgroup characterization. Both support the biological coherence of the findings.

Agreement on central finding of two distinct subtypes (C5-C6, C27). OpenEval evaluates this as a separate high-level conclusion supported by multiple result groups, while peer reviewers integrate it with the detailed subgroup characterization. Both strongly support this core finding.

Agreement on IHC validation (C75-C78, C30, C73-C74, C104). Both support the validation approach and results. OpenEval notes the lack of tumor size difference contrasts with training cohort findings, while peer reviewers emphasize the substantial sample size and clinical applicability without raising this discrepancy.

Agreement on external validation (C73-C74). OpenEval evaluates external cohort validation separately, noting inclusion of non-RPLS liposarcomas may limit comparability. Peer reviewers group this with IHC validation and emphasize the clinical framework without raising concerns about cohort composition.

Agreement on validation methodology (C30, C104). OpenEval evaluates the validation approach as methodologically sound. Peer reviewers integrate this with the broader validation results, emphasizing substantial sample size and clinical applicability.

Agreement on study design and cohort characteristics (C4, C25-C26, C31-C32). OpenEval notes difficulty verifying 'largest landscape' claim, while peer reviewers emphasize the substantial sample size as a strength. Both support the cohort design.

Agreement on cohort comparability (C106). OpenEval supports the lack of significant differences between cohorts as validating the approach. Peer reviewers implicitly accept cohort design through their statement about 'solid and validated methodology.'

Agreement on clinical findings summary (C7-C11). OpenEval notes these claims require verification against detailed results, particularly the extremely high AUC. Peer reviewers accept the prognostic differences and describe the classification as valuable for personalized treatment.

Partial overlap on biomarker classification (C7). OpenEval groups this with other summary claims requiring verification. Peer reviewers emphasize the streamlined classification system and machine learning approach as strengths.

Divergent evaluation on clinical implications (C28-C29, C105). OpenEval rates as UNCERTAIN, noting lack of explicit case examples demonstrating discordance between histological and molecular classifications. Peer reviewers rate as SUPPORTED, emphasizing promise for personalized treatment without requiring specific demonstration of discordant cases.

Divergent evaluation on clinical application claims (C101-C103, C105). OpenEval rates as UNCERTAIN, noting C105's claim about 'precise guidance for surgeons' represents undemonstrated prospective application. Peer reviewers rate as SUPPORTED, viewing the classification as having 'considerable promise' for clinical outcomes.

Agreement on main findings summary (C101-C102) but divergence on clinical application. OpenEval supports the summary of findings but questions the prospective clinical utility claim. Peer reviewers accept the study's novelty and significance without distinguishing between demonstrated findings and prospective applications.

Strong agreement on background and rationale (C1-C3, C12-C24, C81-C85, C101-C102). Both evaluations support the contextualization within prior literature. OpenEval provides detailed assessment of individual claim support, while peer reviewers accept the novelty and significance broadly.

Agreement on literature contextualization (C81-C85). OpenEval notes difficulty verifying 'first clinically applicable' claim but finds it reasonable given IHC validation. Peer reviewers accept the study's novelty without questioning priority claims.
OpenEval evaluates descriptive statistics for IHC validation cohort (C107) as straightforward descriptive data. No corresponding peer review evaluation found for this specific claim.
